A line you typed and never staged was never put in a box.

items: "A hard reset destroyed it, nothing to do." Root cause: git add wrote a blob for every staged version, and the reset removed only the index entries.

git reset --hard origin/main after a forced update. Root cause: it removes the lost commits from the one local branch that still held them; they remain only in reflog entries.

slides.lead: Let's land this. You should now be able to say:
items: Every git add writes a blob; after a hard reset those blobs are dangling and git fsck --lost-found writes them out as files.
Content that was never staged was never an object, and I can show that with git hash-object and git cat-file.
A cleared stash entry is an unreachable merge commit; git stash store puts it back.
After someone's forced push, origin/main@{1} in my clone is the server's old tip.
When status and push disagree, I ask the server with git ls-remote.

A cleared stash entry is an unreachable merge commit; git stash store puts it back.
After someone's forced push, origin/main@{1} in my clone is the server's old tip.
When status and push disagree, I ask the server with git ls-remote.

slides.body: Read sections 13.9 and 13.10 of Chapter 13. Do Lab 12.10, "Broken remote-tracking state, and a corrupt index", in lab-manual/m12-recovery.md.
Today you recovered work that had no name at all, and you used your own clone as the witness after a forced push.

beats.text: Most engineers answer no: a hard reset destroys uncommitted work. Two words first. Staged means recorded with git add for the next commit, the next saved snapshot. And a hard reset puts your files back to the last commit.
beats.tele: Most engineers answer no: a hard reset destroys uncommitted work. Two words first. Staged means recorded with `git add` for the next commit, the next saved snapshot. And a hard reset puts your files back to the last commit.

beats.text: The exact answer has three parts. The version of the file that you staged: yes, it's an object in the repository right now, without a name. An earlier version that you staged before that: also yes. The line you typed after the last git add: no, and you can prove in two commands that no object holds it. Hold on to those two commands.
beats.tele: The exact answer has three parts. The version of the file that you staged: yes, it's an object in the repository right now, without a name. An earlier version that you staged before that: also yes. The line you typed after the last `git add`: no, and you can prove in two commands that no object holds it. Hold on to those two commands.

beats.text: Then a second question from the same afternoon. A teammate forced a push over main, which replaces the server's branch instead of extending it, and two commits by two people are gone from the server. The server kept no record. Who did? You did, if you have fetched before and not thrown it away.
beats.tele: Then a second question from the same afternoon. A teammate forced a push over `main`, which replaces the server's branch instead of extending it, and two commits by two people are gone from the server. The server kept no record. Who did? You did, if you have fetched before and not thrown it away.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. So far in this module every recovery concerned commits, and every commit had a reflog entry somewhere, a line in Git's local log of where each name has pointed. Today you leave that comfort in two directions.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. So far in this module every recovery concerned commits, and every commit had a reflog entry somewhere, a line in Git's local log of where each name has pointed. Today you leave that comfort in two directions.

beats.text: First, down to layer three: work that became an object and has no name at all. A staged blob, the stored content of one file. A stash entry, parked uncommitted work, that was cleared.
beats.tele: First, down to layer three: work that became an object and has no name at all. A staged blob, the stored content of one file. A stash entry, parked uncommitted work, that was cleared.

beats.text: Second, sideways to layer four: the remote side. What your clone knows about the server, when that knowledge is wrong, and how your clone becomes the recovery tool after someone else's forced push.
beats.tele: Second, sideways to layer four: the remote side. What your clone knows about the server, when that knowledge is wrong, and how your clone becomes the recovery tool after someone else's forced push.

beats.tele: recover a cleared stash entry;

beats.tele: repair broken remote-tracking state;

beats.text: restore commits overwritten by someone's forced push from your own clone.
beats.tele: restore commits overwritten by someone's forced push from your own clone.

beats.text: Staged work. On screen, train.yaml from today's demonstration: one edit, then git add. git add writes a blob at the moment you run it. The index is the list of what goes into your next commit.
beats.tele: Staged work. On screen, `train.yaml` from today's demonstration: one edit, then `git add`. `git add` writes a blob at the moment you run it. The index is the list of what goes into your next commit.

beats.text: A hard reset removes the index entries, not the blobs. Nothing names them, so they are dangling, on layer three. A blob has no file name and no date: the name lived in the index entry that is gone. You identify blobs by content. And every git add is a checkpoint that outlives the index entry, so a file staged twice leaves two blobs.
beats.tele: A hard reset removes the index entries, not the blobs. Nothing names them, so they are dangling, on layer three. A blob has no file name and no date: the name lived in the index entry that is gone. You identify blobs by content. And every `git add` is a checkpoint that outlives the index entry, so a file staged twice leaves two blobs.

beats.text: Work typed after the last git add was never hashed. No object holds it. That's the boundary of Git's safety net.
beats.tele: Work typed after the last `git add` was never hashed. No object holds it. That's the boundary of Git's safety net.

beats.text: A dropped or cleared stash. A stash entry is a commit with two or three parents. Dropping it removes its reflog line, so the commit is unreachable. git stash drop prints the ID of what it dropped. git stash clear prints nothing. The stash manual gives a recipe that lists unreachable commits which look like stash entries. The deadline is the one of layer three, and it's shorter than for a rewritten commit: a dropped stash never has a reflog entry to fall back on.
beats.tele: A dropped or cleared stash. A stash entry is a commit with two or three parents. Dropping it removes its reflog line, so the commit is unreachable. `git stash drop` prints the ID of what it dropped. `git stash clear` prints nothing. The stash manual gives a recipe that lists unreachable commits which look like stash entries. The deadline is the one of layer three, and it's shorter than for a rewritten commit: a dropped stash never has a reflog entry to fall back on.

beats.text: A force push seen from your clone. On screen, your main and origin/main agree. Then you fetch after the forced push, and origin/main moves to a commit that doesn't descend from the old one.
beats.tele: A force push seen from your clone. On screen, your `main` and `origin/main` agree. Then you fetch after the forced push, and `origin/main` moves to a commit that doesn't descend from the old one.

beats.text: Your remote-tracking ref has a reflog, and it recorded the value the server had before. origin/main@{1} is the server's old tip. The server itself is a bare repository without reflogs by default, so it can't tell you. A teammate who hasn't fetched since is another witness.
beats.tele: Your remote-tracking ref has a reflog, and it recorded the value the server had before. `origin/main@{1}` is the server's old tip. The server itself is a bare repository without reflogs by default, so it can't tell you. A teammate who hasn't fetched since is another witness.

beats.text: There are two honest repairs.
beats.tele: There are two honest repairs.

beats.text: The second repair is a force push in its own right. Give it an explicit expected value, the forced commit, so that it fails if the server has moved again.
beats.tele: The second repair is a force push in its own right. Give it an explicit expected value, the forced commit, so that it fails if the server has moved again.

beats.text: Remote-tracking refs that can't be trusted. A remote-tracking ref is a local record of the last contact with the server. git status compares two local refs. git push talks to the server. When they disagree, the server is right, and git ls-remote asks it without changing anything. Remote-tracking refs are derived data: remove what is broken and let a fetch write the truth.
beats.tele: Remote-tracking refs that can't be trusted. A remote-tracking ref is a local record of the last contact with the server. `git status` compares two local refs. `git push` talks to the server. When they disagree, the server is right, and `git ls-remote` asks it without changing anything. Remote-tracking refs are derived data: remove what is broken and let a fetch write the truth.

beats.text: When not to do any of this: the reflex "get in sync" with git reset --hard origin/main after a forced update. It removes the lost commits from the one local branch that still held them.
beats.tele: When not to do any of this: the reflex "get in sync" with `git reset --hard origin/main` after a forced update. It removes the lost commits from the one local branch that still held them.

beats.text: Now a picture to keep. In the vault, a staged file is a box that was put on a shelf with a sticky label on the counter, the index entry. The reset swept the counter. The box is on the shelf with no label on it at all: no file name, no date. You find it by opening boxes and reading what is inside.
beats.tele: Now a picture to keep. In the vault, a staged file is a box that was put on a shelf with a sticky label on the counter, the index entry. The reset swept the counter. The box is on the shelf with no label on it at all: no file name, no date. You find it by opening boxes and reading what is inside.

beats.text: A line you typed and never staged was never put in a box. No audit of the vault will find it.
beats.tele: A line you typed and never staged was never put in a box. No audit of the vault will find it.

beats.text: For the remote side, picture two branch offices. Your office keeps a photocopy of the other office's index cards, taken at your last visit, and a ledger of how those photocopies changed. When the other office rewrites a card and keeps no ledger of its own, your photocopy ledger is the only written record of what the card used to say. The model breaks if you treat the photocopy as live. It's only as current as your last fetch.
beats.tele: For the remote side, picture two branch offices. Your office keeps a photocopy of the other office's index cards, taken at your last visit, and a ledger of how those photocopies changed. When the other office rewrites a card and keeps no ledger of its own, your photocopy ledger is the only written record of what the card used to say. The model breaks if you treat the photocopy as live. It's only as current as your last fetch.

beats.text: Six kinds of work. For each one ask the first of the three questions: was it ever an object? Try it now, thirty seconds. Answer for each one. Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Six kinds of work. For each one ask the first of the three questions: was it ever an object? Try it now, thirty seconds. Answer for each one. Say it out loud.

beats.text: The first three say yes. The fourth and fifth say no.
beats.tele: The first three say yes. The fourth and fifth say no.

beats.text: Here is the full table, with what still names each kind of work after the accident. For the fourth and fifth rows you stop using Git at once.
beats.tele: Here is the full table, with what still names each kind of work after the accident. For the fourth and fifth rows you stop using Git at once.

beats.text: sweep.yaml is new and staged. train.yaml has a staged change and a later edit that isn't staged: that is the MM. notes.md is untracked.
beats.tele: `sweep.yaml` is new and staged. `train.yaml` has a staged change and a later edit that isn't staged: that is the `MM`. `notes.md` is untracked.

beats.text: Predict the fate of each of the three files. Say it out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Predict the fate of each of the three files. Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: notes.md survived, because a reset doesn't touch untracked files. sweep.yaml is deleted and train.yaml is back at the committed version. Stop. Classify: staged, so layer three. 🟢 SAFE: git fsck --lost-found writes files under .git/lost-found and changes nothing else.
beats.tele: `notes.md` survived, because a reset doesn't touch untracked files. `sweep.yaml` is deleted and `train.yaml` is back at the committed version. Stop. Classify: staged, so layer three. 🟢 SAFE: `git fsck --lost-found` writes files under `.git/lost-found` and changes nothing else.

beats.text: Predict the number of dangling blobs. Two files were staged.
beats.tele: Predict the number of dangling blobs. Two files were staged.

beats.text: Three blobs for two files, because sweep.yaml was staged twice and each git add wrote a blob. Identify them by content.
beats.tele: Three blobs for two files, because `sweep.yaml` was staged twice and each `git add` wrote a blob. Identify them by content.

beats.text: Both staged versions are back. The third blob, 0697c1f, is the earlier staging of sweep.yaml.
beats.tele: Both staged versions are back. The third blob, `0697c1f`, is the earlier staging of `sweep.yaml`.

beats.text: Now what isn't there. The line early_stopping: true was typed after the last git add.
beats.tele: Now what isn't there. The line `early_stopping: true` was typed after the last `git add`.

beats.text: git hash-object computes the ID that the full file would have had. No object with that ID exists.
beats.tele: `git hash-object` computes the ID that the full file would have had. No object with that ID exists.

beats.text: The boundary of the safety net, drawn in two commands. Those are the two commands from the opening.
beats.tele: The boundary of the safety net, drawn in two commands. Those are the two commands from the opening.

beats.text: The stash, in a second copy of the project.
beats.tele: The stash, in a second copy of the project.

beats.text: No output, no IDs. Here's the recipe from the stash manual. There were two entries. Quick quiz, three options: does it find none, one, or both? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: No output, no IDs. Here's the recipe from the stash manual. There were two entries. Quick quiz, three options: does it find none, one, or both? Say it out loud.

beats.text: One. The recipe ends in --grep=WIP. The default message of a stash is "WIP on" the branch. An entry made with git stash push -m is named "On" the branch and your message, and doesn't match. Leave the --grep out and rely on --merges: a stash entry is a merge commit, and few other unreachable commits are.
beats.tele: One. The recipe ends in `--grep=WIP`. The default message of a stash is "WIP on" the branch. An entry made with `git stash push -m` is named "On" the branch and your message, and doesn't match. Leave the `--grep` out and rely on `--merges`: a stash entry is a merge commit, and few other unreachable commits are.

beats.text: git stash store is 🟢 SAFE: it sets refs/stash and adds one reflog line. The entries are back in the list.
beats.tele: `git stash store` is 🟢 SAFE: it sets `refs/stash` and adds one reflog line. The entries are back in the list.

beats.text: The plus sign and "(forced update)" mean that origin/main didn't move forward: the server's branch was replaced by a commit that doesn't descend from the old one.
beats.tele: The plus sign and "(forced update)" mean that `origin/main` didn't move forward: the server's branch was replaced by a commit that doesn't descend from the old one.

beats.text: Status calls it divergence: ahead 2, behind 1. On the picture, two commits only you have, and one only the server has. Don't "get in sync". Read the evidence.
beats.tele: Status calls it divergence: ahead 2, behind 1. On the picture, two commits only you have, and one only the server has. Don't "get in sync". Read the evidence.

beats.text: origin/main@{1} is the server's old tip, d8a3934. The two ranges are the damage report: two commits by two authors were removed from the server, and one commit, 882b940, was put in their place.
beats.tele: `origin/main@{1}` is the server's old tip, `d8a3934`. The two ranges are the damage report: two commits by two authors were removed from the server, and one commit, `882b940`, was put in their place.

beats.text: The server kept no record. Here the forced commit is legitimate work, so the repair is "keep both".
beats.tele: The server kept no record. Here the forced commit is legitimate work, so the repair is "keep both".

beats.text: The push is a fast-forward, 882b940..d967a92: the server's tip is an ancestor of the merge commit, the commit with two parents that joins both lines. Every clone that already has the old commits, and every CI record that quotes their IDs, stays valid. Rebasing the lost commits onto the forced one would give them new IDs and create duplicates.
beats.tele: The push is a fast-forward, `882b940..d967a92`: the server's tip is an ancestor of the merge commit, the commit with two parents that joins both lines. Every clone that already has the old commits, and every CI record that quotes their IDs, stays valid. Rebasing the lost commits onto the forced one would give them new IDs and create duplicates.

beats.text: Two local refs agree, and the server disagrees. Ask the server.
beats.tele: Two local refs agree, and the server disagrees. Ask the server.

beats.text: Two discrepancies. origin/main holds an ID that the server doesn't have at all, and origin/feature/hybrid-search is reported as a broken ref. The ordinary repair fails.
beats.tele: Two discrepancies. `origin/main` holds an ID that the server doesn't have at all, and `origin/feature/hybrid-search` is reported as a broken ref. The ordinary repair fails.

beats.text: badRefContent names the damaged file. The dangling commit is worth reading: the fetch downloaded the server's new commit and then failed before it could update any ref.
beats.tele: `badRefContent` names the damaged file. The dangling commit is worth reading: the fetch downloaded the server's new commit and then failed before it could update any ref.

beats.text: The ref file is empty. And the newest reflog entry of origin/main has no message. A fetch writes "fetch:", a push writes "update by push". An entry without a message was written by git update-ref from a script or by hand.
beats.tele: The ref file is empty. And the newest reflog entry of `origin/main` has no message. A fetch writes "fetch:", a push writes "update by push". An entry without a message was written by `git update-ref` from a script or by hand.

beats.text: The fetch corrected origin/main with a forced update and recreated the other ref. Status now tells the truth: two commits to push, one to integrate.
beats.tele: The fetch corrected `origin/main` with a forced update and recreated the other ref. Status now tells the truth: two commits to push, one to integrate.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: "A hard reset destroyed it, nothing to do." Root cause: git add wrote a blob for every staged version, and the reset removed only the index entries.
beats.tele: "A hard reset destroyed it, nothing to do." Root cause: `git add` wrote a blob for every staged version, and the reset removed only the index entries.

beats.text: Searching for a staged file by name. Root cause: the file name lived in the index entry; a blob has content only.
beats.tele: Searching for a staged file by name. Root cause: the file name lived in the index entry; a blob has content only.

beats.text: Running the stash recipe with --grep=WIP and concluding that an entry is gone. Root cause: entries made with a message are named "On <branch>: ..." and do not contain "WIP".
beats.tele: Running the stash recipe with `--grep=WIP` and concluding that an entry is gone. Root cause: entries made with a message are named "On <branch>: ..." and do not contain "WIP".

beats.text: git reset --hard origin/main after a forced update. Root cause: it removes the lost commits from the one local branch that still held them; they remain only in reflog entries.
beats.tele: `git reset --hard origin/main` after a forced update. Root cause: it removes the lost commits from the one local branch that still held them; they remain only in reflog entries.

beats.text: Trusting git status about the server. Root cause: status compares local refs, and a remote-tracking ref is a record of the last contact, which can be stale or damaged.
beats.tele: Trusting `git status` about the server. Root cause: status compares local refs, and a remote-tracking ref is a record of the last contact, which can be stale or damaged.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. A data platform team shares main of a question-answering service. On Monday morning one engineer's first fetch prints a plus sign and "forced update". Two commits from Friday, an answer cache by one colleague and its metrics by another, are no longer on the server. In their place is one commit that renames settings keys.

Two commits from Friday, an answer cache by one colleague and its metrics by another, are no longer on the server. In their place is one commit that renames settings keys.

beats.text: She doesn't pull and doesn't reset. She reads the reflog of origin/main and takes the entry before the forced update. Two range listings give her the damage report with authors, and she posts it with full commit IDs. The team decides that the rename is legitimate work, so she merges origin/main into her main, which still has the Friday commits, and pushes.
